How do you discern when something should be prefixed with Die/Der/Das/Den, and so on?

"The food", for example? Why is that "Das Essen" as opposed to "Die Essen" or "Den Essen"?

Every noun in German has a gender. For nouns about people, they are sometimes related to the physical gender of the person, but most often, grammatical gender and sex are not the same.

How do you know which gender a noun is? Memorization. Der/die/das are what we call definite articles; English only has one definite article, "the". When you learn a new noun, you have to learn the definite article along with it. Das Essen is neuter; das Haus is neuter; die Uhr is feminine; der Saft is masculine; die Zeit is feminine; etc. There are some ways to allow you to more accurately guess the correct gender of the noun, e.g. these guidelines, but each noun must be learnt with its respective gender.

In addition to grammatical gender, there are also grammatical cases in German, i.e. nominative, genitive, dative, and accusative. These grammatical cases allow users of the language to more easily distinguish what role which object in a sentence is playing, e.g. direct object, indirect object, prepositional object, etc. Above the above listed definite articles, der, die, and das belong to the nominative case (for the subject of the sentence), and den belongs to the accusative case (for the direct object of a sentence, i.e. what the subject is acting on). For example:

Der Hund beißt den Mann. → The dog bites the man.

The dog is the subject, and the man is the direct object. We know this because der Hund is in the nominative case (for subjects), and den Mann is in the accusative case (for direct objects). If we flip the sentence around:

Den Mann beißt der Hund. → The dog bites the man.

the sentence still means the same because der Hund is still in the nominative case, and den Mann is still in the accusative case. Due to these grammatical cases, German has a more open word order than English or other languages where the meaning of the sentence is heavily dependent on the order of the words.

tl;dr (& ELI5): each noun has a gender, each gender has a definite article (der/die/das), and the definite articles change depending on the case (how the noun is being used in the sentence).
